extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, IP practitioners, policymakers, and attorneys interested in U.S. non-obviousness law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Supreme Court's guidance in KSR v. Teleflex on applying 35 U.S.C. §103 non-obviousness analysis (Graham factors) and the role/limits of the TSM test for patentability. Useful for assessing patent claims and examiner practice regarding combinations of prior-art elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 / Graham factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of non-obviousness must be assessed using the Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the prior art and the claims at issue, and (3) the level of ordinary skill in the relevant art; secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unresolved needs, failure of others) may also be relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court reaffirmed Graham as the main test and described it as expansive and flexible. Apply these factors objectively to determine whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, Suggestion, or Motivation (TSM) test — general principle, not rigid requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is only proved obvious if the prior art, the nature of the problem, or the knowledge of a person having ordinary skill reveals some motivation or suggestion to combine prior-art teachings. However, TSM must not be transformed into a rigid rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSM is a helpful lens to avoid hindsight bias, but courts/examiners should not demand an explicit teaching/suggestion in the references before finding a combination obvious. General principles of TSM may inform the Graham analysis but cannot override it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement must be more than a predictable use of prior-art elements
rubrics_metrics.description: For a combination of known elements to be non-obvious, the improvement must be more than the predictable application of each element according to its established function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the combination was predictable and whether there was an apparent reason to combine the elements; if the combination yields only predictable results, it is likely obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an invention was "obvious to try" is a relevant consideration in the obviousness inquiry, particularly when there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions to a known problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court criticized a narrow understanding that ignored "obvious to try"; when pursuing known approaches with a reasonable expectation of success, a finding of obviousness may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look to interrelated teachings, marketplace demands, and background knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining obviousness may require looking to interrelated teachings of multiple patents, the effects of demands known to the design community or present in the marketplace, and the background knowledge possessed by a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachings need not be precise or explicit; implicit directions in the collective prior art and market/design pressures can point a skilled person toward the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the person having ordinary skill — use of common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The person skilled in the art should not be treated as having no initiative; such a person is capable of using common sense and accounting for particularities of the individual case (e.g., design needs and market demand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and courts should recognize that a skilled artisan can combine known elements using ordinary creativity and common sense; do not require that all combinations be explicitly spelled out in prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner caution: do not overestimate published articles/express prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examiners should not overvalue the presence of published articles or explicit prior-art references to the exclusion of other contextual considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the totality of prior art, marketplace factors, and ordinary skill background rather than relying solely on express citations; avoid formalistic overreliance on isolated published references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid granting patents that would occur in the ordinary course without real innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting patent protection to advances that would occur in the ordinary course without real innovation retards progress and may, for patents combining previously known elements, deprive prior inventions of their value or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a cautious approach when claims are combinations of known elements; ensure the claimed subject matter reflects real innovation beyond expected incremental developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness can be found even without clear TSM
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention may be obvious despite the absence of a clear teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine various prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat lack of an explicit TSM as dispositive for non-obviousness; consider whether the collective prior art and ordinary skill would have led to the claimed invention.
